title: Redefining Instance Matching: A Unified Framework for Part-Aware Matching in Panoptic Segmentation Evaluation
claim: Matching strategy and threshold choice changes which segments count as TP, FP and FN, so standard one-to-one matching can miss credit.
layout: 3 panels (a–c) in a grid, side-by-side matching variants, shared color legend on top
description: A legend row at the top defines four half-and-half circle colors: matched prediction (dark yellow), unmatched prediction or FP (pale yellow), matched ground truth or TP (blue), and unmatched ground truth or FN (pale blue). Below are three panels of overlapping yellow and blue circles. Panel (a) compares One-to-One matching at threshold 0.5 and 0.1, where lowering the threshold turns the center pair into a TP. Panel (b) compares One-to-One and Many-to-One at threshold 0.1, where two small predictions overlap one large blue ground truth. Panel (c) compares One-to-One, One-to-Many and Voronoi region-wise evaluation, with a large yellow prediction spanning two blue circles. The Voronoi panel has teal, pink and orange background regions. Each panel has a bold title above it and the eye goes first to the colored circles.
caption: Comparison of different scenarios where the choice of a matching strategy and threshold impacts PQ significantly. (a) shows a scenario in which at most one predicted segment is matched to a ground truth segment and vice versa. Lowering the threshold counts the center pair as an additional TP. In scenario (b), two smaller predicted segments overlap a bigger ground truth segment: The Many-to-One matching assigns both overlapping predictions to the ground truth, resulting in a higher score. Scenario (c) shows how One-to-One matching does not credit the partial overlap of the prediction with the middle circle, whereas One-to-Many and Voronoi region-wise evaluation match the prediction with the middle circle as well.
abstract: The Panoptic Quality metric is the standard for jointly evaluating instance and semantic segmentation. Its original definition matches predicted and ground truth segments only if their intersection over union exceeds 0.5, a threshold that guarantees a One-to-One matching that is both optimal and unique. Below this threshold, the uniqueness guarantee is lost and multiple matching strategies emerge in a poorly explored problem space. We systematically elucidate this space by recasting segment matching as a constrained bipartite assignment problem. Independently bounding the prediction- and ground-truth-side degrees yields four matching strategies: One-to-One, Many-to-One, One-to-Many, and Many-to-Many. We show that the first three yield interpretable instance-level assignments, whereas Many-to-Many entangles over- and under-segmentation and admits no consistent attribution of errors. These strategies become relevant when instances are fragmented, adjacent objects are difficult to delineate, or annotations are noisy. Central to our framework is a vertex-based accounting of TP, FP, and FN, anchored to ground truth and predicted segments rather than to matching edges. We further show that the framework extends naturally to part-aware panoptic segmentation and illustrate this extension conceptually on biomedical examples. Across configurable case studies we report how different combinations of thresholds and matching strategies behave in practice.
